newsitem.title: INDIA: Cotton - India futures move seen helping trade.
newsitem.headline: Cotton - India futures move seen helping trade.

text.p: India's proposal to resume futures trading in cotton will boost trade and help farmers, the head of a trade organisation said on Friday.

"It's risk protection measure and is in the fitness of things," said East India Cotton Association (EICA) president Suresh Kotak, reacting to the proposal contained in the federal budget for 1997/98 (April/March).
The budget was presented in parliament by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on Friday evening.
"Futures and ready (delivery) are two sides of the same coin," Kotak said. "The decision to allow futures trading in cotton will greatly benefit the cotton economy."
India banned futures trading in cotton in 1966 in a bid to prevent speculation and hoarding and to stabilise prices.
EICA has been demanding resumption of futures trading in cotton in the last few years after India initiated an economic liberalisation programme in 1991.
"The proposal is in line with the liberalisation programme," Kotak said. "It will help cotton growers plan their crop well in advance."
Cotton traders have been arguing that India has now emerged as a surplus cotton producer and that restrictions on trade need to be removed.
The move to allow futures trading in cotton followed the 1994 recommendations of an official committee which called for allowing futures trading in nine commodities, including cotton.
India's cotton crop in 1996/97 (October/September) has been officially estimated at 16 million bales (one bale is 170 kgs) the same as in the previous year.
The government has so far authorised an export of 1.2 million bales in the current season against 1.59 million in 1995/96.
Kotak said EICA had the infrastructure as it had been operating futures trading in the past before it was banned.
